name: OneSpace
headline: Finding a class file should be straightforward.
summary: A research-led communication concept for students and teachers navigating classes, files, and announcements across disconnected apps.
role: UX research, problem framing, flows & interface design
problem: During the shift to online classes, students were being asked to follow different teachers across different communication tools. My starting question was whether bringing communication into one place could make collaboration easier. The more useful question became: how does a student find the right resource when they need it?
process: I began with more than five one-to-one interviews and a virtual discussion with students from different colleges, then used a ten-question survey answered by 127 people. The interviews exposed an adoption mismatch: teachers chose tools they found comfortable, while students inherited the work of keeping up with all of them.

The survey complicated my original assumption. The deck reports that more than half of respondents did not mind using multiple apps, while about 14% found it frustrating. Interest in an all-in-one tool was therefore a signal to explore, rather than proof that every communication tool needed replacing. I translated the findings into a student persona, four problem areas, information architecture, wireframes, and high-fidelity screens.

decisions.title: Organise around a class, then its conversations
decisions.choice: The concept uses spaces and categorised channels, with calls accessible from the chat context.
decisions.reason: A class provides a recognisable place to return to; students should not have to remember which external app a teacher chose.
decisions.tradeoff: This would require institutional participation. A cleaner student interface alone cannot solve fragmented adoption.

decisions.title: Give files and announcements their own home
decisions.choice: I separated a unified file store and an announcements centre from the conversation stream.
decisions.reason: These are the items students need to retrieve later. Their usefulness should not depend on scrolling back through chat.
decisions.tradeoff: Separating destinations adds navigation; useful defaults and clear links back to the class would be essential.

decisions.title: Treat access as part of the product scope
decisions.choice: The prototype explores language support and preferences alongside the core communication screens.
decisions.reason: The interviews describe uneven comfort with technology. Familiar structures and understandable language matter as much as consolidating features.
decisions.tradeoff: The deck also explores watch support and parental controls. Today I would defer those until the core retrieval journey had been tested.

outcome: I designed spaces for classes, channels for conversation, and separate places for files and announcements. The prototype covers the wider communication flow, but those two destinations are the part I would carry into a first release. The project stopped at a prototype; usability testing was the next step.
reflection: The survey made me question my original all-in-one idea. Being willing to try a new app did not mean students needed every tool replaced. I would start with finding a file and catching an announcement, then test whether those tasks are enough to justify another app.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask students to retrieve an assignment, identify the latest announcement, and join the correct class; compare task success and recovery with their current workflow.
Proposed scope: pilot one class before adding institution-wide migration, parental controls, or a second device. Include teacher setup effort in the evaluation.

name: uMatter
headline: A clearer first step towards professional support.
summary: A 14-hour team challenge exploring a more approachable route from mental-health awareness to finding and booking professional support.
role: Team lead · UX research & design
context: Team Elementors · Pixel Perfect UI/UX Challenge
problem: The challenge brief focused on making access to mental-health support more efficient. I led the UX research and design contribution for Team Elementors, working with Pratik Manjrekar on UI design and Nidhi S Kamath on UI and graphic design. Our task was to turn a broad and sensitive brief into a coherent mobile journey within fourteen hours.
process: We used a shortened Double Diamond process to divide research, structure, and interface work. Our ten-question survey received 65 responses. The deck reports that almost half wanted professional help while remaining anonymous, and almost 89% had never visited a therapist. Those responses guided the concept toward privacy expectations and an approachable first step.

We supplemented the survey with article research, assembled a persona, mapped the flow, and progressed from wireframes to high-fidelity screens. The sample was exploratory: the deck does not document recruitment, a representative population, or a controlled evaluation. I treat its percentages as directional responses from this sample.

decisions.title: Build a path to support, rather than promising diagnosis
decisions.choice: The concept connects expert discovery, an expert profile, appointment selection, and payment.
decisions.reason: Breaking access into visible steps gives a person a clearer idea of what happens after they decide to seek help.
decisions.tradeoff: Although the challenge brief used the word diagnosis, these screens do not demonstrate clinical diagnosis or treatment effectiveness.

decisions.title: Put trust information before commitment
decisions.choice: Expert detail and review-based trust cues sit before calendar booking and payment in the documented journey.
decisions.reason: A person needs to understand who they are approaching before being asked to commit time or money.
decisions.tradeoff: Ratings alone do not establish professional competence. Credential verification would need its own operational process.

decisions.title: Explore lower-pressure ways to engage
decisions.choice: The team added awareness content, stories, and lighter activities alongside the booking journey.
decisions.reason: Not every visitor is ready to book immediately. The concept offers a way to explore the topic before taking that step.
decisions.tradeoff: More destinations can dilute the primary route to professional support; I would test whether they help or distract.

outcome: We completed the mobile concept within the fourteen-hour challenge, from onboarding and expert profiles to appointment selection and payment. I led the team and the UX research and design. Pratik Manjrekar contributed UI design; Nidhi S Kamath contributed UI and graphic design. Our final artifact was a prototype, not a clinical service.
reflection: The survey raised a question we could not resolve in the challenge: how does someone stay anonymous while booking an accountable professional service? I would work through what is shared at each step before adding more features to the concept.
nextSteps: Proposed validation: test whether participants understand what is private, what a provider can see, and whether the product offers booking or diagnosis.
Proposed iteration: add clear provider credentials, consent and cancellation information, then evaluate the booking journey with appropriate professional input.

name: MuCoin
headline: Making the first budget less of a form.
summary: A personal-finance onboarding concept that turns income, expenses, and savings goals into a reviewable starting picture.
role: Product framing, onboarding flow & interface rationale
problem: A useful financial picture depends on personal information that takes effort to recall and can feel uncomfortable to share. I structured MuCoin around a sequence that asks for income, fixed expenses, variable expenses, savings goals, and a final review. The design challenge was to make that effort understandable and correctable.
process: The original write-up explains the flow screen by screen, including privacy links, expense summaries, editable goals, and review behaviour. It also defines proposed KPIs for each stage. The design centres on repeatable entry, useful summaries and a review that remains editable.

The source mentions a small user subset when discussing the label Saving Goals, but gives no sample size, protocol, or measured comparison. I treat that as informal input. The numerical completion and drop-off figures in the appendix are targets, not results.

decisions.title: Ask for a small, repeatable unit of information
decisions.choice: The income stage starts with amount and source, while fixed and variable expenses use similar entry patterns.
decisions.reason: A familiar pattern lets the person concentrate on their finances instead of relearning the interface at every step.
decisions.tradeoff: A short form still needs room for irregular income, uncertain estimates, and multiple sources; simplicity cannot mean forcing inaccurate answers.

decisions.title: Show a useful picture before onboarding ends
decisions.choice: The expense stages return a chart, summary table, total, and relationship to income.
decisions.reason: Summaries create opportunities to notice a missing entry or an implausible total while the information is still fresh.
decisions.tradeoff: A chart is only as good as its inputs. It should communicate an estimate when the person is unsure, rather than imply financial precision.

decisions.title: Make confirmation an editable checkpoint
decisions.choice: The review groups income, expenses, and goals into three collapsible, editable sections.
decisions.reason: Being able to inspect and correct information gives the person control over what they submit.
decisions.tradeoff: The old rationale claims review ensures complete task success. That is a hypothesis to test; a confirmation screen cannot guarantee it.

outcome: I designed a five-stage setup flow for income, expenses, savings goals and review. The entry patterns repeat, the summaries give something back along the way, and the final review stays editable. The accompanying KPI figures describe targets for a future test, not measured completion or drop-off.
reflection: A useful setup should leave someone with a financial picture they understand. I would pay close attention to corrections: noticing and fixing an amount can be a better outcome than finishing the form quickly with the wrong numbers.
nextSteps: Proposed measures: completion per stage, time to a usable summary, errors noticed during review, and understanding of what happens to entered information.
Proposed study: compare a short path with optional detail against the original sequence. Include irregular income and skipped estimates rather than testing only ideal inputs.

name: GetMetaData
headline: An SEO panel you can actually scan.
summary: A browser-extension redesign exploring information hierarchy for people with different levels of SEO experience.
role: Competitive review, information architecture, wireframes & UI
problem: GetMetaData exposes a page’s SEO elements, but a dense readout makes it difficult to see what needs attention. The original review describes small text, weak information architecture, and a repeated-output bug. My task was to improve inspection without stripping away the useful detail or export capability.
process: I compared SEO META in 1 CLICK, All in One SEO Analyzer, and Detailed SEO Extension alongside GetMetaData. I used my own portfolio as the common test page and looked at functionality, usability, SEO information, and documentation. This kept the content context consistent, although one website could not represent every page structure.

I then used two persona perspectives—an SEO engineer and a small-business/content-marketing user—to frame different reading needs, before creating wireframes and a high-fidelity prototype. The deck does not document interviews validating those personas, so I use them as design lenses rather than research findings.

decisions.title: Retain information depth, improve the route through it
decisions.choice: The redesign explores a clearer hierarchy for metadata, headings, images, structured data, and links.
decisions.reason: An inspector should help a person locate relevant evidence before asking them to interpret a full page of metrics.
decisions.tradeoff: A more segmented interface can make cross-category comparison harder. Testing should include jumping between related issues.

decisions.title: Compare tools in a controlled content context
decisions.choice: I reviewed the competing extensions against the same portfolio page.
decisions.reason: Using one common page makes differences in presentation easier to discuss without changing the underlying website at every comparison.
decisions.tradeoff: The review is a historical snapshot on one site, not a current market ranking or a large performance benchmark.

decisions.title: Separate interface redesign from a functional repair
decisions.choice: The review records duplicated output as a bug, while the deliverable remains an interface prototype.
decisions.reason: Making data easier to read would not fix incorrect or repeated extraction. The two problems need separate acceptance criteria.
decisions.tradeoff: The prototype can demonstrate hierarchy and navigation; it cannot prove the extraction bug was resolved.

outcome: I completed the competitor review, wireframes and high-fidelity prototype. The redesign groups the extension’s information into clearer destinations while retaining its depth and export workflow. I recorded the repeated-output bug separately; an interface prototype could not establish whether extraction had been fixed.
reflection: The next test should use real inspection tasks: find a missing description, check headings, compare related issues and export the findings. That would tell me more than asking whether the new panel looks cleaner.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a novice and an experienced practitioner to locate a missing title, inspect image descriptions, and export their findings.
Proposed acceptance criteria: correct extraction without duplication, clear reading order, and useful handling of a page with unusually long or missing values.

name: Steve Wilson
headline: Let the work lead the portfolio.
summary: An early portfolio concept exploring typography, project browsing, and a repeatable case-study template.
role: Visual direction, page structure & interface concept
problem: A portfolio has to communicate what a designer does, offer a convincing sample of their work, and make contact straightforward. This early concept uses the fictional Steve Wilson identity to explore that sequence through a home page, work listing, project-detail template, and contact destination.
process: The available evidence is a four-page visual artifact, including a long project-detail template. It contains sample copy, mock project names, placeholder results, and a sample client attribution. Those are layout content, not my client history or achieved results.

I organised the pages so that the introduction establishes the designer’s role, the work listing exposes project categories and tools, and the detail template reserves space for the problem, process, outcome, and lessons. No original research or testing record accompanies it.

decisions.title: Use typography to establish the first impression
decisions.choice: The concept combines a large name treatment with a restrained dark background and a bright accent.
decisions.reason: The visual hierarchy gives the identity a clear point of entry before visitors scan services or projects.
decisions.tradeoff: A strong name treatment cannot replace useful positioning copy; I would make the designer’s particular value more specific.

decisions.title: Separate browsing from deep reading
decisions.choice: The work listing acts as an index, while project details have a longer narrative structure.
decisions.reason: Visitors can skim the portfolio before deciding which story deserves more attention.
decisions.tradeoff: A listing only helps if its labels explain the work rather than relying on unfamiliar project names.

decisions.title: Give each project the same narrative spine
decisions.choice: The template includes role, problem, process, results, takeaways, and final product.
decisions.reason: A repeated structure helps a reviewer compare contributions across projects.
decisions.tradeoff: In the archive, much of that structure is empty sample content. A template is useful scaffolding, not evidence of a completed case study.

outcome: I designed a homepage, work index, project-detail template and contact page around the fictional Steve Wilson identity. The exercise helped me explore the difference between scanning a body of work and reading one project closely. Names, client credits and result figures in the original template are sample content.
reflection: I would keep the clear browsing structure and rewrite the project pages around actual decisions. A well-proportioned template is useful, but the writing and evidence inside it are what make a portfolio convincing.
nextSteps: Proposed iteration: replace the sample project with one real story, then test whether a reviewer can identify the role, central decision, and outcome in a short scan.
Proposed UI review: verify contrast, keyboard navigation, responsive reading order, and a concise contact path before implementation.

name: Gloria Furniture
headline: A furniture shop organised around the room.
summary: A furniture storefront concept connecting room-led browsing, product comparison, and purchase actions.
role: Visual design & storefront information hierarchy
problem: Furniture is both a visual and a practical purchase. The original Gloria concept tries to support inspiration at the top of the page, category exploration in the middle, and concrete products with prices further down. The design question is how to make those modes feel like one useful shopping path.
process: The surviving PDF is a single long storefront design, not a research report. I reviewed its hero, category imagery, quality messaging, product cards, and service links to make the underlying structure explicit. The archived dollar prices, warranty copy, and contact details are sample storefront content, not verified business facts.
This is a retrospective reading of the design. The available artifact does not establish customer interviews, a checkout implementation, or commercial performance.

decisions.title: Start with inspiration, then offer more specific choices
decisions.choice: The hero leads into visual categories before the featured Home Decor and Furniture groups.
decisions.reason: A shopper can begin with a broad interest and progressively narrow to a product, instead of meeting a full catalogue immediately.
decisions.tradeoff: The path would need descriptive category labels and accessible images; atmosphere alone does not tell a shopper where to go.

decisions.title: Make product cards comparable
decisions.choice: The featured groups repeat name, price, image, Add to Cart, and Buy Now treatments.
decisions.reason: A stable card structure supports scanning across products and makes purchase actions predictable.
decisions.tradeoff: Two equally prominent purchase actions can compete. Today I would test a primary product-detail path before offering immediate purchase everywhere.

decisions.title: Keep practical reassurance near the shopping journey
decisions.choice: The concept includes a quality band and footer links for stores, warranty claims, and custom requests.
decisions.reason: Furniture decisions often require service and fulfilment information as well as appealing photography.
decisions.tradeoff: Those claims need real policies and product information. The visual concept alone cannot establish quality or a working support service.

outcome: I designed a storefront landing page that moves from room inspiration into categories and comparable product cards. Prices and service information sit alongside the imagery so browsing has a practical direction. The artifact is a visual concept; it does not include a working checkout.
reflection: I would next add the details someone needs before buying furniture: dimensions, materials, stock and delivery coverage. Those are more useful at this stage than another promotional section.
nextSteps: Proposed task: find a product within a budget, compare two options, and explain delivery expectations. Record missing information as well as completion.
Proposed iteration: build a product-detail page and a narrow-screen catalogue, using real product data and one clearly prioritised action.

name: Fun Cruises Goa
headline: Choosing a boat before making an enquiry.
summary: A yacht-rental landing-page concept organised around capacity, price, and the next enquiry.
role: Landing-page structure, fleet browsing & visual design
problem: A visitor choosing a boat needs to know whether it fits their group and budget before making an enquiry. The Fun Cruises Goa artifact contains the building blocks for that decision: a prominent booking action, a description of the experience, fleet filters, and listings with seating capacity and starting hourly prices.
process: I reviewed the original long-page design as a visitor journey from initial interest to a suitable fleet option. The available PDF shows the landing and fleet-discovery surface. It does not include completed reservation, payment, or availability states, so I describe the scope as discovery and enquiry.

The rates, capacities, address, and response-time copy visible in the old concept are historical design content. This case study uses their placement to explain hierarchy, rather than presenting them as current offers.

decisions.title: Bring decision criteria into the fleet list
decisions.choice: The design offers seating, price-order, and boat-type controls, with capacity and starting rate on individual listings.
decisions.reason: A visitor should be able to rule out unsuitable options without opening every boat’s detail page.
decisions.tradeoff: Filters depend on consistent inventory data. Empty results and combinations that return no suitable boat would need explicit handling.

decisions.title: Support both ready-to-book and exploratory visitors
decisions.choice: The concept has a hero booking action and an enquiry route alongside fleet details.
decisions.reason: Some visitors know what they want; others need clarification before committing. The page makes both next steps available.
decisions.tradeoff: Booking, getting a quote, and learning more can become competing calls to action. I would clarify which action each listing should lead to.

decisions.title: Use imagery with practical content
decisions.choice: Fleet photographs sit beside capacity, starting price, and short descriptions.
decisions.reason: The images convey the experience while the text helps establish whether the option is suitable.
decisions.tradeoff: A starting hourly price does not communicate the full cost. Minimum duration, inclusions, fees, and availability would need to be explained next.

outcome: I redesigned the landing and fleet-browsing page around boat type, capacity and starting rate. The imagery introduces the experience, while the listings give visitors something concrete to compare before enquiring. Availability and a completed reservation flow are outside the delivered concept.
reflection: An enquiry should not look like a confirmed booking. I would make that distinction explicit, then add the inclusions, accessibility details and cancellation terms needed to discuss a trip. Prices in the original design are historical concept content.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a visitor planning for a group to choose a suitable option, explain the expected cost, and identify what remains to confirm.
Proposed extension: add a boat-detail page with availability, inclusions, accessibility information, cancellation terms, and a clear enquiry handoff.

name: BNI Goa
headline: Meet the chapter. Know how to take part.
summary: A chapter-website concept that connects the organisation’s purpose, the people behind it, and a first visit.
role: Information hierarchy & website visual design
problem: A person considering a business network needs to understand its purpose, who participates, and how to take a first step. The BNI Victory Goa design brings those questions into a local chapter website with an invitation, organisation overview, leadership section, member directory, and contact form.
process: The available PDF is a long-page visual concept. I reviewed the sequence from the hero invitation through purpose and people to contact. The artifact does not contain an interview report, launch evidence, or a membership funnel.

The member cards repeat placeholder identities and informal sample biographies. The overview also contains network-wide statistics. Neither is evidence of chapter growth or my project impact, so those details are not promoted as results here.

decisions.title: Give the visitor a concrete first step
decisions.choice: The hero uses a Get Invited action instead of making the organisation overview the only starting point.
decisions.reason: An invitation turns interest in networking into an understandable next action.
decisions.tradeoff: The next screen would need to explain meeting expectations and eligibility; a button label alone does not establish that service.

decisions.title: Make the organisation visible through its people
decisions.choice: Leadership and member-card patterns occupy distinct sections.
decisions.reason: The directory can help a visitor understand the kinds of businesses represented and who is responsible for the chapter.
decisions.tradeoff: Repeated mock content weakens credibility. Production would require member permission, verified biographies, and a reliable update process.

decisions.title: Keep purpose and contact in the same journey
decisions.choice: The page connects the chapter overview and mission to a form and local contact details.
decisions.reason: A visitor can move from understanding the organisation to asking a practical question without searching elsewhere.
decisions.tradeoff: The long single-page structure would benefit from a tighter summary and explicit links to meeting details.

outcome: I designed a chapter-site concept that brings the organisation’s purpose, leadership, members and invitation into one sequence. Reusable member patterns give the page a structure that could grow with the chapter. The archived design contains sample biographies and is not a record of actual member results.
reflection: Before expanding the directory, I would confirm the local chapter information, member permissions and visitor process. The people and meeting details need to be accurate for the invitation to be useful.
nextSteps: Proposed iteration: replace all sample biographies with verified chapter content and explain the visitor-meeting process before the invitation action.
Proposed evaluation: ask a prospective visitor what the chapter does, whether it is relevant to their business, and what will happen after they request an invitation.

name: IRCTC
headline: The train search comes first.
summary: An independent homepage concept exploring the hierarchy between a primary booking task and a large set of secondary services.
role: Task hierarchy & interface redesign concept
problem: A railway homepage serves many audiences, but searching for a train is a clear primary task. My independent IRCTC concept places the booking form prominently while retaining entry points for PNR status, vacancies, concessions, and related travel services. The challenge is hierarchy: helping the common task stay visible without erasing important exceptions.
process: The source is one full homepage design, not a documented end-to-end booking redesign. I evaluated the visible grouping of From, To, Date, Class, and Quota, the surrounding service links, and the separation of holiday content below the search area.

There is no original usability study or live implementation in the provided material. Dates, phone numbers, and offers in the mockup are sample or historical interface content, not current travel guidance.

decisions.title: Keep the core journey fields together
decisions.choice: The concept groups origin, destination, travel date, class, and quota in a single booking panel with a visible Search action.
decisions.reason: The person can form a complete query in one recognisable task area.
decisions.tradeoff: The retained panel still contains many specialised options. Today I would test how to reveal less common settings without hiding essential access needs.

decisions.title: Distinguish a current journey from trip inspiration
decisions.choice: Related services and curated holidays appear beneath the primary search region.
decisions.reason: A person trying to book a known route should not have to read promotional content first.
decisions.tradeoff: The holiday cards remain text-heavy. Visual separation helps hierarchy but does not by itself solve page density.

decisions.title: Retain explicit entry points for adjacent rail tasks
decisions.choice: PNR status and chart/vacancy shortcuts remain accessible near the booking area.
decisions.reason: People returning to manage an existing journey have a different task from people searching for a new one.
decisions.tradeoff: The homepage only establishes entry points. It does not demonstrate those destination flows or their error handling.

outcome: I created an independent homepage concept with a clear train-search area and grouped entry points for secondary rail services. The work concentrates on the starting task. Search results, changing availability and the rest of the booking flow were not part of this concept.
reflection: I would take the same hierarchy into a difficult journey: no seats available, a changed fare or an unsuitable route. A quieter homepage only helps if the following screens make those decisions understandable too.
nextSteps: Proposed test: find a train, check an existing journey, and locate a concession option; compare discovery and mistakes without assuming that a shorter visual scan means a successful booking.
Proposed extension: add no-results, changing availability, route correction, keyboard navigation, and narrow-screen form states.

name: Nitya Nanda
headline: A photography site that leaves room for the photographs.
summary: A photography portfolio concept with a deliberately restrained interface and two clear ways into the work.
role: Portfolio structure & visual design
problem: A photography portfolio needs to show the work before asking visitors to read a long introduction. The Nitya Nanda concept explores a restrained structure with About, Work, and Contact destinations, an image-led opening, and separate professional and freelance collections.
process: The available source is a single long visual concept. I traced how the page introduces the photographer, groups the work, and leads to the contact form. The listed shoots, locations, and credentials are illustrative portfolio content; the artifact does not substantiate them as real commissions.
This retrospective draws design observations from the page itself. No original audience research, client engagement record, or booking measurements accompany the concept.

decisions.title: Keep the navigation vocabulary small
decisions.choice: The page repeats About, Work, and Contact around an image-led presentation.
decisions.reason: These are familiar questions for someone considering a creative professional and make the portfolio easy to orient within.
decisions.tradeoff: Repeated navigation should help orientation rather than consume space. Today I would test a single persistent version on smaller screens.

decisions.title: Separate two ways of reading the portfolio
decisions.choice: Professional and freelance work have their own grouped image collections with captions.
decisions.reason: The distinction gives visitors a route based on the kind of commission they are considering.
decisions.tradeoff: The grouping is a design assumption. Real enquiries might be better served by subject, service, or photographic style instead.

decisions.title: Give the visual journey a practical endpoint
decisions.choice: A short contact form follows the portfolio, with additional work and consultation links.
decisions.reason: Someone convinced by the images should have a direct route to starting a conversation.
decisions.tradeoff: The concept stops at submission. A complete service needs clear expectations, error messages, and confirmation of what happens next.

outcome: I designed a restrained portfolio with professional and freelance collections, a small navigation system and a contact destination. The layout lets visitors browse images before deciding to make an enquiry. The biography and photography credentials in the concept are illustrative.
reflection: I would spend the next pass on selecting images, writing useful captions and checking loading performance. The interface has already done enough when it helps someone understand the work and find a way to get in touch.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask visitors choosing a photographer to identify a relevant body of work and start an enquiry; observe which category language they expect.
Proposed implementation: responsive image sizes, descriptive alternatives, keyboard access, and a complete form confirmation and error flow.

name: Arkitype
headline: Change a token. See what it changes.
summary: A working design-system studio that links foundations, component behaviour, previews, and exports through one model.
role: Product idea, design-system UX & interaction direction
problem: A palette, a component library, and a handoff document can each look convincing while disagreeing with one another. I approached Arkitype as a connected workspace: decisions about colour, type, space, shape, and motion should remain visible in the components and artifacts they produce.
process: I framed the workspace around eight connected design areas, rather than a compulsory wizard. A designer should be able to revisit a foundation while considering a component and still understand what depends on that decision.

The UX goal is continuity: foundations, component states, previews, and handoff should feel like parts of one system. The current 90-component library is product scope; it does not establish that a new user understands the workspace.

decisions.title: Use dependencies to guide, rather than enforce a sequence
decisions.choice: Foundations, assets, components, and preview remain accessible, with relationships expressed as Built from and Lands in links.
decisions.reason: The navigation reflects iterative design work instead of pretending every system starts and ends in the same order.
decisions.tradeoff: An open workspace gives less automatic direction. First-use guidance must help a person find a useful starting point.

decisions.title: Keep design changes consistent across surfaces
decisions.choice: The preview, component workspace, and handoff reflect the same design decisions.
decisions.reason: A change should carry through to the places a team actually uses, rather than depend on repeated manual updates.
decisions.tradeoff: A designer needs to know which properties carry through and which need review before handoff.

decisions.title: Let people inspect appearance and behaviour
decisions.choice: The studio distinguishes controlled component specimens from interactive previews.
decisions.reason: A design system needs comparable states and realistic behaviour. One view cannot do both equally well.
decisions.tradeoff: Interactive examples add state and complexity; the underlying specimen must remain predictable for documentation and export.

outcome: I shaped Arkitype around the relationship between foundations, component states, previews and handoff. The beta brings those surfaces into one workspace, with a documented library of 90 components. The design question I still want to test is whether a new user can follow a change through the whole system.
reflection: I would ask a designer to change a foundation, find the affected component states and prepare a handoff. If they need a second explanation at every step, the workspace is still making them carry too much of the system in their head.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a designer to start from one brand colour, adjust a component, and produce a usable handoff. Record confusion, corrections, and output mismatches.
Proposed measure: time to the first coherent system and the number of inconsistencies discovered after export, with a defined task and baseline.

name: AppleCider
headline: Room to sketch before committing to a design.
summary: A sketch-like wireframing workspace that carries rough screens into clickable prototypes and editable handoff artifacts.
role: Product idea, sketching workflow & interaction design
problem: Early design conversations can become arguments about polish before the underlying idea is settled. I framed AppleCider around an intentionally unfinished visual language: the speed and social permission of a sketch, with the editing capabilities of a digital workspace.
process: I separated the experience into a welcoming introduction, a files workspace, and the editing canvas. This gives each moment a clear task: understand the tool, find the work, then explore an idea.

The design loop is sketch, revise, demonstrate, and hand off. Components, undo, snapping, links, and export matter because they let someone change their mind without starting again. Formal user validation remains a next step.

decisions.title: Make the unfinished quality deliberate
decisions.choice: Wobbly strokes, a sketch-like type treatment, and three visual styles preserve a low-fidelity feel.
decisions.reason: The interface should invite changes to the idea before encouraging arguments about pixel-level finish.
decisions.tradeoff: A sketch aesthetic can also reduce legibility. Labels, focus states, and interactions still need the clarity of a serious tool.

decisions.title: Keep the work portable
decisions.choice: The files surface stores documents locally and supports a plain project-file export, alongside image and vector outputs.
decisions.reason: A person should be able to keep and move their work without an account or a proprietary cloud workflow.
decisions.tradeoff: Browser storage is device-specific and can be cleared. File ownership needs an understandable backup and export path.

decisions.title: Carry structure into the next artifact
decisions.choice: The handoff offers editable output and a written specification, alongside the clickable prototype.
decisions.reason: The transition from a rough screen to a working conversation should preserve the decisions already made.
decisions.tradeoff: Generated structure is a starting point. Placeholder copy and sketch styling should not be presented as finished product requirements.

outcome: I used an intentionally rough visual language across the canvas, files workspace and prototype flow. The product includes 250 sketch components and editable handoff formats, so an early idea can move forward without pretending to be a finished interface.
reflection: The roughness needs to make revision easier, not make the tool harder to use. I would test whether someone can change a screen, demonstrate its flow and hand it over without losing the decisions they already made.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: give participants an early product idea, ask them to revise it after feedback, and then explain the exported prototype to someone else.
Proposed measure: time to the first understandable screen, effort to revise its structure, and corrections needed after export.

name: PlanIt
headline: A trip plan that leaves room for people.
summary: A browser-based itinerary workspace for overlapping plans, different travellers, and different time zones.
role: Product framing, group-planning journeys & interaction design
problem: A group trip is not a single ordered checklist. Different people arrive at different times, attend parallel activities, and move between places. I approached PlanIt as several useful views of one plan, with a board for thinking and a time model for checking whether that plan can work.
process: I distinguished tentative ideas from scheduled commitments. The canvas supports exploration, while itinerary, timeline, map, and people views help the group understand the consequences of a plan.

The key interaction is the deliberate move from arrangement to schedule. Pins protect an existing commitment; loose ideas can stay undecided. The UX needs to explain what Resolve changes and make conflicts understandable.

decisions.title: Give the board a clear but limited grammar
decisions.choice: Day frames, ordering, and connectors convey meaning; loose cards can remain uncommitted ideas.
decisions.reason: A planning surface needs room for uncertainty instead of assigning a date and time to everything immediately.
decisions.tradeoff: Spatial meaning must be taught. A frame or connector that looks decorative can otherwise change a plan unexpectedly.

decisions.title: Make scheduling an intentional action
decisions.choice: Tidy turns the existing itinerary into a board; Resolve reads the board back into the schedule.
decisions.reason: A person should know when arrangement becomes a commitment. Automatic rearrangement would undermine the value of a free board.
decisions.tradeoff: Two explicit directions add a concept to learn, so the product needs visible feedback about what changed and why.

decisions.title: Protect decisions the planner has already made
decisions.choice: Pinned times win, untouched loose cards opt out, and resolution only moves times forward when constraints require it.
decisions.reason: Automation should respect existing intent and explain an impossible plan rather than silently rewrite it.
decisions.tradeoff: A conservative resolver may leave conflicts unresolved. The interface must help the person decide what to relax.

outcome: I designed the board, itinerary, timeline, map and people views as different ways of working with the same trip. Scheduling is deliberate, pinned commitments stay protected, and conflicts remain visible. That behaviour is the part of PlanIt I would explain first to a new group.
reflection: I would try the planner with a late arrival, two parallel activities and a booking that cannot move. The useful test is whether people can predict what Resolve will change and spot a conflict before it becomes a problem on the trip.
nextSteps: Proposed study: plan a trip with parallel sessions, a pinned departure, and travellers in two zones; ask participants to predict Resolve before using it.
Proposed measure: unexpected schedule changes, correctly identified conflicts, and confidence explaining the final plan.

name: Earthlog
headline: What is happening around this place?
summary: Explore earthquakes, weather, and the night sky from one place on a globe.
role: Experience framing, information hierarchy & map interactions
problem: A place can have recent earthquakes, old incident records, current weather, and predicted sky events. Bringing them onto one map makes exploration easier, but can also make very different information look equally current and reliable.
process: I framed two ways into exploration: start from a place, or follow an interesting event to its location. Both routes should arrive at a readable local picture, rather than another layer to decode.

Freshness and uncertainty are part of the information hierarchy. An observation, an older open record, and a forecast need different labels so the map does not make them look equally current or certain.

decisions.title: Start with a place or a question
decisions.choice: People can search for a place, select the globe, or follow an event shortcut.
decisions.reason: Someone may be curious about the latest earthquake without knowing where it happened.
decisions.tradeoff: Every route needs to lead back to the same place context.

decisions.title: Show when the information was observed
decisions.choice: The documented event model uses observation recency instead of treating every open incident as current.
decisions.reason: A source’s administrative status can outlive the actual event. The label should communicate what is known.
decisions.tradeoff: Freshness rules remain approximations; source links and timestamps must stay visible.

decisions.title: Explain the limits beside the result
decisions.choice: Eclipse paths, station passes, and aurora layers carry model limitations in the documented product.
decisions.reason: A compelling map should not appear more precise than the calculation behind it.
decisions.tradeoff: Caveats can overwhelm the visual story, so they belong beside the relevant result rather than only in documentation.

outcome: I brought place search and event discovery together on the globe. A visitor can start with a location or an event, then inspect dates, sources and the relevant model limits. I kept that context close to the result rather than making the globe’s appearance carry the explanation.
reflection: I would ask someone to explain one result in their own words: what happened, when it was observed and where the information came from. Finding an event is only part of the task.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: ask visitors to distinguish a recent observation from a modelled forecast and locate the source behind each result.
Proposed measure: correct interpretation of freshness and uncertainty, alongside success finding a relevant local event.

name: HexChess
headline: Learning chess on a different board.
summary: A 91-cell chess variant designed around guided learning, readable interaction, and games that survive interruptions.
role: Learning journey, onboarding & game interactions
problem: A hexagonal board changes movement patterns enough to make familiar chess knowledge unreliable. I designed HexChess around learning by trying: clear targets, feedback on moves, and a route into untimed practice instead of expecting a beginner to absorb a rules document first.
process: I connected a six-part introduction to the first practice game. A learner should encounter a rule on the board, try a move, and carry that understanding into play.

I treated interruption and sharing as parts of the experience. A saved game needs a clear return path, and a correspondence link needs to explain that the other person replies with an updated game rather than joins a live room.

decisions.title: Make movement teachable on the board
decisions.choice: Lessons give a specific target, neutral markers, retries, and progress based on actual practice.
decisions.reason: A learner can connect a rule to a move instead of memorising abstract directions.
decisions.tradeoff: Move previews and legal moves serve different purposes; the interface must explain when inspection ignores king safety.

decisions.title: Keep assistance appropriate to the context
decisions.choice: Hints and takebacks belong to computer practice; human games remove assistance and pause controls.
decisions.reason: Learning support should not silently change the rules of a friendly competitive game.
decisions.tradeoff: Assistance rules need to be clear to both players; the interface is not evidence of tournament-grade enforcement.

decisions.title: Describe sharing accurately
decisions.choice: Correspondence links carry move history and require an updated reply after a turn.
decisions.reason: People should understand whether they are entering a synchronized room or receiving a game snapshot.
decisions.tradeoff: Long histories create long URLs, and a shared snapshot is readable by anyone given the link.

outcome: I connected the 91-cell board to six guided lessons, practice, saved sessions and correspondence sharing. Legal-move feedback helps explain the unfamiliar geometry where the move happens. I have not measured whether the lessons improve learning.
reflection: I would follow a new player from a lesson into their first game. A completed tutorial is less useful evidence than seeing them recognise a move, recover from a mistake and continue without an explanation.
nextSteps: Proposed study: observe a new player complete a piece lesson and use the same movement unaided in practice.
Proposed checks: reload during a game, resume offline, and exchange a correspondence reply while confirming both players understand the snapshot model.

name: DashF1
headline: Follow the driver. Keep the race in view.
summary: A race dashboard connecting timing, track context, and replay while distinguishing measured data from estimated positions.
role: Dashboard hierarchy, driver focus & information design
problem: A race weekend produces more signals than a person can follow at once, and the available feed changes between live and replay sessions. DashF1 uses one shared driver focus across the timing tower, map, and detail views so the dashboard supports a question rather than a wall of independent charts.
process: I organised the experience around one driver focus. Timing, track context, and detail panels should answer related questions without requiring the same selection repeatedly.
I separated live and replay expectations. When a position is estimated, the label belongs near the moving marker; missing coverage should be understandable at the moment someone tries to use it.

decisions.title: Carry one selection through the dashboard
decisions.choice: Choosing a driver updates the relevant map and telemetry context.
decisions.reason: The person should not have to repeat the same selection in several panels.
decisions.tradeoff: The relationship must remain clear when the selected driver retires or a particular data channel is unavailable.

decisions.title: Let the mode determine the promise
decisions.choice: Live mode shows supported channels; fuller replay data becomes available through a separate path.
decisions.reason: Missing data should change the interface’s promise instead of being replaced with plausible-looking numbers.
decisions.tradeoff: A mode change can alter familiar panels, so the dashboard needs an understandable explanation.

decisions.title: Label an estimate at the point of use
decisions.choice: The documented free-feed map derives position from mini-sector timing and gaps, and calls it estimated.
decisions.reason: Visual continuity is useful, but it should not be mistaken for location precision the feed does not provide.
decisions.tradeoff: Race interruptions and stale timing can challenge the estimate; smooth motion must not conceal those limits.

outcome: I organised timing, track position, telemetry and replay around one selected driver. The selection carries across panels, while session mode and data coverage explain what each view can show. Estimated positions need to stay visibly different from recorded data.
reflection: I would check what someone believes when a feed is incomplete. An empty or estimated view should be understandable without making them leave the race to read a technical explanation.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a viewer to follow a battle and explain which values are observed, historical, or estimated.
Proposed checks: missing telemetry, stale updates, interrupted streams, safety-car periods, and the transition back to replay.

name: Hued
headline: One colour. A reason to look closer.
summary: A daily photography prompt with a shared constraint, on-device scoring, and a warm visual language.
role: Product concept, creative loop & visual direction
problem: A broad prompt to be creative can be harder to act on than a small constraint. Hued gives everyone the same daily colour and asks them to find and photograph it in the real world. The product connects a simple creative action to a repeatable daily rhythm.
process: I shaped the concept around one shared colour and a small creative invitation: notice it in the world, photograph it, and see other interpretations. The daily boundary needs a clear local explanation.

A quiet, warm interface keeps the photographs in front. Scores and streaks are supporting feedback; whether they encourage curiosity or pressure is a question for evaluation, not an established habit-formation result.

decisions.title: Make the prompt shared and specific
decisions.choice: One date-derived colour creates a common constraint for the day.
decisions.reason: A small, concrete invitation can make starting easier and make different responses interesting to compare.
decisions.tradeoff: A UTC boundary may feel surprising across time zones; the deadline needs to be understandable locally.

decisions.title: Keep the creative result in the foreground
decisions.choice: The feed emphasises photographs within a quiet, warm visual system.
decisions.reason: The person’s interpretation of the colour should carry more attention than surrounding interface decoration.
decisions.tradeoff: Ranking and streaks can compete with exploration; their value needs to be judged from behaviour and feedback.

decisions.title: Treat scoring as guidance with limits
decisions.choice: Colour matching runs locally; suspicious-image heuristics are documented as tentative rather than proof.
decisions.reason: A score can provide feedback without pretending to reliably determine how an image was made.
decisions.tradeoff: Lighting, camera processing, and scene composition affect colour. An unexplained penalty can feel arbitrary.

outcome: I centred the app on a shared daily colour, a photograph and feedback on the attempt. The warm interface gives the photographs most of the attention; scores, the feed and streaks support the daily activity. Participation and the scoring experience still need user evaluation.
reflection: I want the prompt to encourage noticing things, not just protecting a streak. I would ask people what they chose to photograph and how they interpreted the score before deciding whether to make the competitive features more prominent.
nextSteps: Proposed study: compare how people interpret the prompt and score under different lighting conditions, including whether they understand a low score.
Proposed measure: repeat participation with self-reported creative value; evaluate deadline understanding across time zones.

name: Yuva Panaji
headline: An event page is only the beginning.
summary: A community website and operations portal linking event discovery with registration and committee workflows.
role: Information architecture, registration & volunteer workflows
problem: A community organisation needs a public account of what it does and a practical way to run the next event. The reviewed Yuva source brings those responsibilities together: public discovery and registration on one side, event administration and committee workflows on the other.
process: I mapped the service from public event discovery and registration through committee review and the attendance desk. Participants and volunteers need different views of the same event information.
The design priority is continuity: information entered on a registration form should remain useful when a volunteer checks someone in, corrects a record, or prepares a printed list.

decisions.title: Connect discovery to the event’s operational record
decisions.choice: The public registration journey and admin roster belong to the same event model.
decisions.reason: A committee should not have to reinterpret a public sign-up into a separate attendance workflow.
decisions.tradeoff: Custom events need flexible fields without making every registration form equally complex.

decisions.title: Give public and committee users different surfaces
decisions.choice: Visitors see event and organisation information, while management workflows sit behind admin access.
decisions.reason: The interface should reflect different responsibilities and information needs.
decisions.tradeoff: A clean separation in navigation is only part of the requirement; permissions and data handling must be verified independently.

decisions.title: Include the work that happens away from the screen
decisions.choice: The documented system supports desk attendance sheets and spreadsheet exports.
decisions.reason: Community operations often happen at an event desk, where a printable list can be more useful than another dashboard.
decisions.tradeoff: Exported files can become stale. The workflow should explain when a printout was produced and how corrections return to the system.

outcome: I connected public event information and registration with the committee’s follow-up work: rosters, corrections, exports and attendance. The public website and operations portal have different jobs, but the information needs to carry from one to the other.
reflection: I would review the handoff at an actual event: who checks a registration, who corrects it and what the attendance desk receives. That is where duplicate entry and outdated lists become visible.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: follow one event from discovery through registration, roster correction, and check-in with both participant and committee perspectives.
Proposed measure: duplicate corrections, incomplete registrations, and handoff effort at the event desk, with a documented baseline.

name: DeckForge
headline: A PDF deck you can work with again.
summary: A browser presentation tool that turns PDF drawing instructions into editable objects, animation, and presenting workflows.
role: Product idea, editing experience & presentation flows
problem: A PDF preserves how a slide looks but usually loses the convenient objects a presenter wants to edit. DeckForge approaches that gap as a reconstruction problem: recover meaningful text, images, and vector objects, then let a person work with them rather than repainting a screenshot.
process: I framed the editor around objects a presenter can recognise: a text block, a logo, a shape, or a chart. A technically selectable fragment is not useful if its meaning is unclear.
The flow needs to explain what can be edited, preserve a usable slide when recovery is limited, and distinguish live presentation pacing from an exported recording.

decisions.title: Make layers correspond to recognisable objects
decisions.choice: Paths are grouped into likely logos, dividers, shapes, and chart series, while text is reconstructed into blocks.
decisions.reason: An editable layer is useful only if the person recognises what it represents.
decisions.tradeoff: Object recovery is heuristic. Preserving appearance can be more valuable than forcing misleading editability.

decisions.title: Let a presenter control the pace
decisions.choice: Animations can wait for an advance action, while timed outputs play sequentially.
decisions.reason: A live talk and an exported recording need different behaviour from the same slide.
decisions.tradeoff: That difference must be visible before export so the presenter knows what an audience will receive.

decisions.title: Keep the core document workflow local
decisions.choice: PDF reconstruction and editing run in the browser; phone pairing has a separate connection mechanism.
decisions.reason: Local processing supports a lightweight workflow and avoids requiring a document-upload service.
decisions.tradeoff: Phone pairing still uses signalling, and some remote features exchange preview frames. The privacy explanation should distinguish those paths.

outcome: I organised recovered slide content into recognisable objects that can be edited, sequenced, presented and exported. Some content remains an image, so the interface needs to explain what was recovered and what can actually be changed.
reflection: I would use a difficult deck to test the explanation, not just a clean example. Someone should be able to tell why one element is editable and another is not, then choose a workable next step.
nextSteps: Proposed benchmark: import a defined set of native-text, scanned, multi-column, and dense-vector PDFs; record editability and visible fidelity separately.
Proposed study: revise a real slide and present it, measuring manual corrections and surprises between editor, audience view, and exported output.

name: Vansh Vriksha
headline: Family connections with a source to follow.
summary: A community genealogy archive that treats relationships, provenance, and contribution review as parts of the same experience.
role: Archive concept, relationship exploration & contribution UX
problem: A family archive is not simply a diagram of names. Relationships can be disputed, spellings vary, and historical records represent some people much better than others. Vansh Vriksha is structured around exploring those connections while preserving the basis for a record.
process: I treated the archive as a set of connected records with several entry points: a person, a family, a village, or a relationship. The UX should help someone follow a connection without losing its source.
The demonstration content lets the experience be explored; it is not verified family evidence. Missing records, uncertain relationships, and contribution review need visible explanations.

decisions.title: Model relationships beyond a simple tree
decisions.choice: The graph includes family unions and parent links rather than forcing every connection into one hierarchy.
decisions.reason: A plain tree can misrepresent remarriage and half-sibling relationships. The data model needs to preserve the actual relationship.
decisions.tradeoff: A more faithful model is harder to lay out and explain, especially on small screens.

decisions.title: Keep a record’s basis alongside the record
decisions.choice: The documented model includes provenance and versioned family files.
decisions.reason: Someone reading a family claim should have a way to understand where it came from and how it changed.
decisions.tradeoff: A source field does not guarantee accuracy. Disagreement and corrections still need a human review process.

decisions.title: Separate contribution from publication
decisions.choice: Visitors can submit without an account, while a maintainer reviews additions.
decisions.reason: A low-friction contribution path can coexist with an accountable published archive.
decisions.tradeoff: Moderation becomes an operational commitment; the interface should communicate what happens while a submission waits.

outcome: I designed relationship browsing, record context and contribution review as connected parts of the archive. A person can explore a connection and inspect the basis for it. The demonstration records show the interaction; they do not establish verified family histories.
reflection: I would make gaps in the archive easier to recognise. A missing branch can mean incomplete records, so it should not quietly look like a statement about which families or people matter.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: ask a family contributor to submit a relationship, inspect its provenance, and correct a disputed connection.
Proposed review: distinguish demonstration records from sourced records in every public count and assess living-person privacy across search and sharing.

name: PreMoney
headline: A bank message is not always a clean transaction.
summary: A personal-finance app that converts bank and UPI messages into reviewable transactions, categories, and summaries.
role: Product concept, transaction review & correction flows
problem: Manual expense entry asks people to repeat information already present in transaction alerts. PreMoney explores a more useful starting point: extract likely transactions from messages, then make uncertainty and correction part of the workflow.
process: I framed the core journey as evidence, suggested transaction, review, correction, and summary. A person should be able to understand why an alert became a record and recover when the interpretation is wrong.

Privacy explanations belong alongside optional categorisation and synchronisation. The experience needs to make those choices understandable without relying on a blanket claim that all processing stays on the device.

decisions.title: Prefer an uncertain result to a fabricated detail
decisions.choice: The parser lowers confidence when a field is uncertain and records when a merchant is unresolved.
decisions.reason: A plausible but incorrect financial record can be harder to notice than a clear request for review.
decisions.tradeoff: Conservative parsing can miss legitimate alerts. The product needs a recoverable route for false rejections.

decisions.title: Make correction useful beyond a single transaction
decisions.choice: Transaction editing and review make suggested categories and corrections inspectable.
decisions.reason: Repeated mistakes should become easier to diagnose than manually editing the same pattern forever.
decisions.tradeoff: A learned rule can also propagate a wrong assumption, so its effect must remain inspectable.

decisions.title: Treat enrichment as a separate data decision
decisions.choice: Optional categorisation and synchronisation need a separate explanation from reading a transaction alert.
decisions.reason: People need an understandable account of which data is used by which feature.
decisions.tradeoff: The product documentation describes external processing paths; disclosures and controls need review before making privacy promises.

outcome: I designed a route from the original message to a suggested transaction, correction and summary. The important part is being able to inspect an entry’s origin and fix it when the interpretation is wrong. Accuracy needs to be evaluated against a defined set of messages.
reflection: I would start with a wrong amount, a duplicate alert and a message that is not a transaction. If correcting those cases is difficult, adding more charts will not make the financial record more dependable.
nextSteps: Proposed benchmark: use a consented, redacted alert corpus to measure false accepts, false rejects, duplicate errors, and corrections by bank format.
Proposed release review: document the external-processing and sync paths, then test whether a person understands and controls them.

name: SoundBox
headline: The song waits until you are ready.
summary: A piano-learning app that connects familiar songs, visible keys, and listening-based progression at the player’s pace.
role: Learning concept, practice flow & feedback design
problem: Someone who wants to play a familiar song may not yet read notation or keep up with a timed lesson. SoundBox starts from the song and a picture of the keyboard, then waits for the player to produce the expected note or chord.
process: I organised the learning experience around a song, an approachable arrangement, and a repeatable passage. The default practice mode waits for the learner instead of making the person chase a clock.

Listening feedback needs a clear ready, heard, and retry state. Recognition reliability has not been established across real instruments and rooms, so recovery deserves as much design attention as successful progression.

decisions.title: Make progression depend on readiness
decisions.choice: The default mode advances after the expected musical input rather than at a fixed tempo.
decisions.reason: A beginner can concentrate on finding the right movement without constantly falling behind the interface.
decisions.tradeoff: Recognition errors can still interrupt the experience, so recovery and a clear input state are essential.

decisions.title: Offer more than one way into a song
decisions.choice: Chord, simplified, and full-melody arrangements support different levels of challenge.
decisions.reason: A learner can begin with something recognisable and increase complexity when ready.
decisions.tradeoff: An automatically simplified arrangement still needs musical review; lower note density is not always easier to play.

decisions.title: Support repetition without punishment
decisions.choice: Section looping and restrained progress mechanics accompany local practice history.
decisions.reason: Practice often means repeating one difficult passage, not completing a song from the beginning.
decisions.tradeoff: Streaks and XP can distract from learning if they reward activity without meaningful progress.

outcome: I designed practice around visible keys, listening-based progression and repeatable passages. Different arrangements give learners more than one way into a song. The app lets them stay with a difficult note; recognition reliability and learning outcomes need separate evaluation.
reflection: I would watch the full practice loop: listening, finding a key, playing it, interpreting the feedback and trying again. A passage-completion count would miss much of what makes that experience frustrating or useful.
nextSteps: Proposed study: observe a beginner learning one short passage with the default wait mode, including how they recover from missed detections.
Proposed benchmark: test recognised notes and chords under varied room noise, microphones, and keyboards; report false advances separately from missed inputs.

name: Wheelie
headline: Different starting points. One place to meet.
summary: A group-riding beta that connects rendezvous planning, rider location, helmet voice, and ride summaries.
role: Service idea, coordination journeys & interaction constraints
problem: Group riding begins before everyone reaches the same road. People start in different places, need a meeting point, and can lose contact after setting off. Wheelie brings planning, group location, and helmet voice into one service concept, with large, simple controls as an explicit design constraint.
process: I framed three moments: meeting before a ride, coordinating with the group, and looking back afterwards. Each moment needs a different level of detail and attention.

The constrained physical context informs large targets, restrained choices, and clear connection states. The next evaluation belongs in stationary or controlled settings; the beta is not evidence of safe in-motion interaction.

decisions.title: Begin with a rendezvous, not just a destination
decisions.choice: The service computes a meeting point for people starting from different places.
decisions.reason: The group’s coordination problem exists before shared navigation can begin.
decisions.tradeoff: A fair computed point may not be a suitable physical stopping place; people need to review the suggestion.

decisions.title: Reduce reliance on precise gestures
decisions.choice: The design calls for large primary targets and simple tap/drag interactions.
decisions.reason: A constrained physical context should affect the interface model from the start.
decisions.tradeoff: Large buttons alone cannot establish safe in-motion use. Evaluation should begin in stationary or controlled settings.

decisions.title: Separate coordination from reflection
decisions.choice: Live map and voice support the current group; ride summaries serve the post-ride story.
decisions.reason: Different moments deserve different information and levels of attention.
decisions.tradeoff: Social summaries can create incentives around speed; the content priorities deserve review before wider use.

outcome: I organised the beta around meeting before a ride, coordinating with the group and reviewing the ride afterwards. Meeting points, group location, helmet voice and summaries serve those different moments. Large controls are a design intention, not evidence that the app is safe to operate while moving.
reflection: I would move as much setup as possible into the time before the ride. The next checks belong in a stationary or controlled setting, with particular attention to connection status and anything that asks the rider to look away.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: test rendezvous planning and headset controls while stationary, then assess attention demands under an appropriately controlled protocol.
Proposed checks: poor connectivity, location permission changes, unavailable voice, battery use, and clarity about whether rider positions are stale.

name: Matinee
headline: Less scrolling. A film worth saving.
summary: A cinema-tracking product connecting discovery, a personal watchlist, ratings, and locally generated recommendations.
role: Discovery concept, browsing journeys & responsive UX
problem: Finding a title and choosing what to watch are related but different tasks. Matinee connects browsing with a personal record of saved and watched titles, using that history to shape the next set of suggestions.
process: I connected browsing with the personal record of saved, rated, and watched titles. The design question is how that history can make the next discovery session more relevant without becoming repetitive.

Language preferences, variety, and recognisable film/series labels inform the browsing experience. Navigation and poster density should adapt to the screen while keeping the selected title and next action clear.

decisions.title: Keep a title’s type visible
decisions.choice: Movie/series identifiers appear in discovery and combined lists.
decisions.reason: A person choosing a two-hour film has a different commitment from someone starting a series.
decisions.tradeoff: A badge helps scanning but does not replace runtime and season information near a decision.

decisions.title: Let personal history influence discovery
decisions.choice: Ratings and watch patterns feed a local scoring process, with controls against repetitive franchises or genres.
decisions.reason: Recommendations should reflect preference without becoming a list of near-duplicates.
decisions.tradeoff: A scoring rule is not evidence of relevance. Cold-start and unexpected recommendations need separate evaluation.

decisions.title: Adapt the structure to the screen
decisions.choice: Phone navigation becomes a side rail at wider sizes, and poster grids expand.
decisions.reason: The same task can use space differently without turning a larger screen into a stretched phone layout.
decisions.tradeoff: Density should still preserve readable text, meaningful focus order, and a clear selected title.

outcome: I connected discovery, watchlists, history and ratings so previous choices can inform the next one. Film and series context, language preferences and variety all have a place in that flow. I have not established a measured recommendation-accuracy result.
reflection: I would ask whether people found something they wanted to watch, not just something they clicked. I would also check whether suggestions become too familiar after a few ratings.
nextSteps: Proposed study: compare a new profile with a rated-history profile and ask participants why each suggestion feels relevant or repetitive.
Proposed measure: useful selections, unwanted repetition, and confidence choosing across preferred languages.

name: BirthSky
headline: Turn a time and place into a sky to keep.
summary: An astronomy-inspired experience that turns a time and place into a customisable star-map wallpaper.
role: Experience concept, input journey & visual direction
problem: A star map can be a technical chart or a personal object. BirthSky connects a simple biographical prompt to a visual reveal, then gives the person control over labels and the final wallpaper format.
process: I organised the experience into a familiar prompt, a personal reveal, optional exploration, and a keepsake. Name, date, time, and place give the abstract sky a recognisable starting point.
The reveal needs understandable inputs. Unknown birth times, time zones, and any collection of personal details deserve clear explanations before a precise-looking image encourages confidence.

decisions.title: Begin with a recognisable personal question
decisions.choice: A short form collects the time and location before revealing the sky.
decisions.reason: The input makes an otherwise abstract astronomical chart meaningful to the person requesting it.
decisions.tradeoff: Unknown birth times and historical time zones require careful explanation; a precise-looking map can still rest on uncertain inputs.

decisions.title: Make annotation a choice
decisions.choice: The result supports alternative modes and toggles for constellation lines and names.
decisions.reason: A person may want to learn from the sky or simply use it as a visual keepsake.
decisions.tradeoff: Switches need clear effects without making the result feel like a complex scientific console.

decisions.title: Design the output as part of the journey
decisions.choice: Phone and desktop wallpaper downloads follow the reveal.
decisions.reason: A useful result should fit where the person intends to use it.
decisions.tradeoff: Export must preserve legibility and composition across aspect ratios rather than just scale one screenshot.

outcome: I designed the journey from entering a time and place to adjusting a star map and exporting a wallpaper. Annotation and output choices let the person decide what belongs in the final image. Time uncertainty and data handling need to stay clear throughout.
reflection: I would make it easier to work with an approximate birth time before adding another visual style. The result is personal, so the person should understand which inputs shaped it and what those inputs can reasonably tell them.
nextSteps: Proposed validation: compare known dates and locations with an authoritative sky reference, including historical daylight-saving and time-zone cases.
Proposed iteration: explain any logging before submission and make uncertain birth-time choices visible in the final result.
