name: ScaleSee
headline: How much bigger? Show the difference.
summary: A visual comparison tool that turns quantities into scenes while keeping the meaning of scale explicit.
role: Visual explanation, comparison journeys & interaction design
problem: A ratio can be mathematically clear and still be difficult to picture. ScaleSee turns two quantities into a shared visual comparison, choosing a representation that fits the kind of quantity instead of using the same chart for everything.
process: I selected a visual reference appropriate to each kind of quantity: a ground line for height, nesting for land, or a shared course for speed. The reference is part of the explanation.

An extreme ratio creates a useful design tension: showing true scale can make one quantity nearly disappear. A compressed alternative needs an explicit label that remains with a shared comparison or exported image.

decisions.title: Choose the picture to fit the quantity
decisions.choice: Height shares a ground line, land can be nested, and speed uses a common course.
decisions.reason: A meaningful reference can make a ratio easier to interpret than a generic bar.
decisions.tradeoff: Every visual metaphor introduces assumptions; those assumptions need to be stated where they affect the comparison.

decisions.title: Keep scale transformations explicit
decisions.choice: True scale and logarithmic scale are separate modes.
decisions.reason: When a small quantity almost disappears, that can be the honest answer; a compressed alternative should declare the change.
decisions.tradeoff: A log view can make a scene more legible while reducing intuitive proportionality.

decisions.title: Let the comparison leave the tool
decisions.choice: A URL carries the selected comparison and an image export preserves the current drawing.
decisions.reason: An explanation is more useful when someone can bring it into the conversation that prompted it.
decisions.tradeoff: An exported image needs labels and scale context because it no longer has interactive controls beside it.

outcome: I matched comparison scenes to the quantity being explored and kept the scale mode explicit. Sharing and image export let a comparison leave the tool with its context. Extreme ratios still need testing for correct interpretation.
reflection: Sometimes a proportional picture is too small to read and an adjusted view is easy to misread. I would check whether someone can identify the scale mode and explain what the picture does to the original numbers.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask readers to estimate the ratio before and after each view, including an extreme comparison and a logarithmic one.
Proposed check: confirm labels, units, assumptions, and scale mode survive in every shared or exported artifact.

name: Where Would I Be…?
headline: Where would this place be as the plates move?
summary: An interactive globe that lets a chosen place move with a plate-motion model and makes the model’s limits part of the story.
role: Experience framing, interaction sequence & spatial explanation
problem: Plate motion is slow enough to be invisible in everyday life and large enough to reshape a world over time. This project gives that scale a personal anchor: choose a place, move the clock, and follow the ground beneath it.
process: I gave the opening one task: choose a place. A time control and a short result then introduce motion, with optional detail kept out of the main globe.
The visual story needs to carry its qualification with it. Constant-motion extrapolation can invite exploration, but the result should not read as a reconstruction or prediction of the continents.

decisions.title: Give each stage one main task
decisions.choice: Choose a place first, then explore time, with optional comparison later.
decisions.reason: A clear sequence can make a complex subject approachable without presenting every control at once.
decisions.tradeoff: Progressive disclosure should not hide the model’s most important qualification until after someone has formed a false impression.

decisions.title: Protect the space where the answer is drawn
decisions.choice: The design keeps the main globe clear and groups controls in a bottom dock.
decisions.reason: The selected point and its path are the explanation; a floating panel over them would compete with the result.
decisions.tradeoff: A dock must adapt to available height so it does not consume the same space on a small screen.

decisions.title: Make the scientific boundary legible
decisions.choice: The source describes plate movement as a constant-motion extrapolation with increasing limits over long horizons.
decisions.reason: Personal storytelling can encourage exploration without claiming to know the future shape of continents.
decisions.tradeoff: A smooth animation can still imply certainty, so the qualification belongs near the time result.

outcome: I used a chosen location as the starting point for exploring time on the globe. Time controls, comparison and optional layers support the exploration, while the model limit stays near the result. The long-term path is an extrapolation, not a geological forecast.
reflection: I would ask someone to explain why the point moves and why the long-term path is conditional. The interaction should leave them with a useful question about plate motion, not misplaced confidence in a prediction.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask a visitor to describe what changed and what assumptions the model makes after a short exploration.
Proposed checks: narrow-screen globe visibility, reduced-motion behaviour, keyboard interaction, and whether uncertainty stays visible at extreme dates.

name: The Blog
headline: A home for my writing, in the form it needs.
summary: An editorial site with a browser-based publishing workflow for poems, essays, fiction, and serial writing.
role: Editorial structure, reading experience & author workflow
problem: A personal writing practice should not require a technical deployment ritual for every post. The Blog connects a reading experience with a browser editor that handles content, images, drafts, and publishing through a familiar form.
process: I framed writing, reviewing, and publishing as separate commitments. The editor should support the author’s work without requiring technical knowledge of how a post reaches the website.

The reading experience follows the form of the writing: poetry keeps its line breaks, while topics and series help a reader continue. Publication feedback should make draft and live states easy to distinguish.

decisions.title: Give publishing a clear state
decisions.choice: Draft and published are separate states, with a deliberate release action.
decisions.reason: Writing and releasing a piece are different commitments and should remain distinguishable.
decisions.tradeoff: Publishing can take time. The author needs clear confirmation of what is saved and what is live.

decisions.title: Let the content form affect the layout
decisions.choice: Poetry preserves line breaks and an appropriate verse treatment, while ordinary articles retain a reading layout.
decisions.reason: The way a piece is written can be part of its meaning.
decisions.tradeoff: Formatting conventions must be discoverable in the editor rather than depend on hidden technical knowledge.

decisions.title: Make ongoing writing navigable
decisions.choice: Topics and series connect related pieces within the editorial structure.
decisions.reason: A reader should be able to follow a thread without knowing the order it was published.
decisions.tradeoff: The documented title-based series matching is convenient but implicit; a visible series field would make mistakes easier to avoid.

outcome: I gave poems, essays and ongoing stories a reading structure suited to each form. The publishing flow separates drafts from release, while topics and series help a reader continue. Poetry keeps its line breaks instead of being squeezed into an ordinary article template.
reflection: I would make draft status and series membership more explicit in the editor. Those small details affect whether I can publish the right version and whether someone can find the next part of a story.
nextSteps: Proposed evaluation: publish a draft, update an existing post, and add a series instalment without using development tools.
Proposed measure: accidental publication, broken links after slug edits, and clarity about whether the latest save is live.

name: The Office Games
headline: Get everyone in. Keep the round moving.
summary: A team-trivia experience exploring quick room entry, visible roles, and shared game state for a short social break.
role: Social game concept, room journey & turn-taking UX
problem: A short team game loses momentum when people are unsure how to join or whose turn it is. The reviewed Office Games module centres on a simple room flow, a lobby, team roles, and a visible answering/stealing sequence.
process: I mapped the reviewed trivia journey from joining a room to understanding teams, turns, answering, and stealing. The broader games catalogue is outside the evidence available for this case study.
The UX needs to explain the connection mode before a group commits to a game. Trying a local demonstration and joining colleagues on separate devices are different experiences.

decisions.title: Make joining a small action
decisions.choice: A four-letter room code and a player name provide a concise entry path.
decisions.reason: A social break should spend more of its time playing than explaining setup.
decisions.tradeoff: A short code still needs clear invalid-room and full-room handling, and does not establish secure identity.

decisions.title: Expose responsibility in the game state
decisions.choice: The interface distinguishes answering and stealing teams, active players, and scores.
decisions.reason: People need to see who can act and why the round is waiting.
decisions.tradeoff: Role-based interaction becomes confusing if waiting states or connection loss are not explained.

decisions.title: Keep connection mode understandable
decisions.choice: The setup distinguishes a local demonstration from connected play.
decisions.reason: A demo can help someone try the game, but should not promise multi-device play it cannot provide.
decisions.tradeoff: A connected game needs clear waiting, conflict, reconnection, and host-recovery states.

outcome: For the trivia flow documented here, I focused on room entry, teams, scores and the answering-and-stealing sequence. The interface gives the group a shared view of who can act next. Local demo mode and connected play need different expectations.
reflection: I would run a short session and pay attention to the pauses: joining, waiting for a team, recovering a connection and changing the host. The answer screen is only one part of whether the break feels easy to join.
nextSteps: Proposed study: run a short trivia session with several participants and record setup explanations, confused turns, and waiting time.
Proposed checks: separate-device joining, reconnection, duplicate actions, host departure, and a clearly labelled local demo mode.

name: Forma
headline: Health readings with the context attached.
summary: A native Android health app that brings activity, sleep and personal trends together while making sources, missing data and experimental estimates visible.
role: Product concept, health-data journeys & interaction design
status: Native Android app · experimental wellness estimates
problem: A watch can collect more measurements than a person can comfortably interpret. A number also changes meaning when it is old, incomplete, imported or estimated. I framed Forma around a daily overview that stays useful without making uncertain data look more reliable than it is.
process: I organised the experience around five destinations: Today for a daily overview, Sleep for the recorded night, Move for activity and workouts, Trends for comparison, and Health for the measurement library. The native app is the product; the React version in the repository is a design preview.

The data constraints shaped the UX. Samsung Health must share records through Health Connect, permissions can be partial, and not every watch measurement is available. Connection setup therefore needs to explain availability rather than treat an empty reading as a failure or a zero.

The later function audit separated Devices from Your data, moved optional personal tools into settings, removed controls without a working purpose, and put formulas behind expandable details. The archived screens illustrate the native visual direction; the audit and current source establish the later navigation and scope. This is an artifact-based retrospective, without a participant study or clinical validation.

decisions.title: Distinguish recorded, missing and estimated values
decisions.choice: Keep source labels and measurement times attached to readings. Preserve gaps in histories, identify sample data, and distinguish sleeping heart rate from a recorded resting-heart-rate value.
decisions.reason: A recent refresh does not mean a sensor reading is recent. People need to understand what a value represents before comparing it with yesterday or using it to interpret their day.
decisions.tradeoff: These labels add density. The hierarchy has to keep essential provenance visible while leaving longer explanations available on demand.

decisions.title: Let a score open into its explanation
decisions.choice: Show the score and its contributing values first, then offer the calculation and diagnostics in an expandable sheet. Recovery requires recorded sleep and a usable baseline vital; missing inputs can leave the estimate unavailable.
decisions.reason: An unexplained score can look authoritative. Showing its inputs makes the estimate inspectable and lets the interface explain why the same score can accompany different activity records.
decisions.tradeoff: Transparency does not validate the model. Sleep, recovery and body-energy estimates remain experimental wellness interpretations, distinct from Samsung proprietary scores and medical assessment.

decisions.title: Separate connecting a device from managing data
decisions.choice: Devices leads with connection state and the next available action. Your data contains coverage, export, optional import and local reset. Targets and personal tools have their own settings paths.
decisions.reason: Someone trying to connect a watch should not have to interpret a coverage report or navigate file-management controls before granting access.
decisions.tradeoff: Separating the tasks adds destinations. Clear names and back paths matter, particularly when permissions are partial or a watch has not synced.

outcome: I organised the native app around a daily overview, dedicated sleep and movement views, histories and a searchable health library. A score opens into its contributors; device setup and data management have separate destinations. The estimates remain experimental, and Samsung sharing depends on the device and permissions.
reflection: Separating Devices from Your data made the next action clearer. I would now check whether someone can explain an unavailable or older reading as readily as a complete one, and whether they can find the inputs behind a score.
nextSteps: Proposed study: ask people to distinguish sample, shared, direct-watch, older and unavailable readings, then explain what an experimental recovery score does and does not mean.
Proposed device checks: follow granted, denied and partial-permission journeys on a Samsung phone and watch, including delayed sync, expired direct readings and corrected history.
Proposed measures: connection-task completion, mistaken interpretations of missing data, and success finding a score explanation or exporting records.

name: OhCaptain
headline: Sail your ship. Coordinate the fleet.
summary: A 3-v-3 naval game exploring shared command, role-specific decisions and a combat interface that keeps the sea in view.
role: Game concept, captain/operator journeys & tactical interface design

facts.label: captain and two operators per crew

problem: In OhCaptain, sailing and firing are only part of the job. Each crew shares supplies, but its captain decides how to spend them. Operators need to request help while both roles keep track of a changing battle. I framed the interface around the next decision a player can actually make.
process: I separated the crew journey into choosing a station, entering solo play or assembling a room, deploying, and managing the battle. A captain still sails and fights; the extra responsibility is distributing shared supplies. Operators request upgrades or repairs rather than spending the treasury themselves.

The documented Clear Deck revision gives combat a compact score/clock, fleet-alive counts, hull status and a persistent map. Spending moves into the Fleet drawer, while the expanded overview holds rosters, recent events and relay details. Warnings compete for a small number of attention slots instead of becoming a wall of banners.

I reviewed the local playable build, documentation and awareness rules. Solo play with AI fill and peer-to-peer rooms are distinct product paths. Online scope depends on a host keeping the page open; the prototype has no dedicated match service or host migration. Rule checks and seeded scenarios do not establish balance or usability with human crews.

decisions.title: Make responsibility visible before deployment
decisions.choice: Offer Captain and Vessel Operator as distinct stations. Captains distribute shared supplies through the Fleet drawer; operators use the same crew context to request an upgrade or repair.
decisions.reason: A shared resource needs a clear decision owner. Role-specific actions let people understand why they can request something but cannot buy it directly.
decisions.tradeoff: The captain can become a bottleneck while also sailing and fighting. Pending requests need to remain discoverable without forcing a panel over combat.

decisions.title: Keep essential battle state on the field
decisions.choice: Keep the score, clock, relay balance, fleet-alive counts, hull and corner map available. Put spending in a drawer and detailed rosters, events and defenses in the expanded overview.
decisions.reason: The map helps connect local action to the relay objective. Separating routine awareness from deliberate inspection leaves room to aim and navigate.
decisions.tradeoff: An overview can interrupt action. Solo overview pauses the match; online play continues, so players need to understand that distinction. The prototype targets keyboard and mouse rather than claiming a touch-control experience.

decisions.title: Give urgent feedback a limited attention budget
decisions.choice: Show at most one off-screen enemy bearing and reserve one text cue for critical hull, safe healing or an endangered home relay. Limit outgoing damage feedback to two numbers and keep routine radio outside combat.
decisions.reason: An alert is useful only if it helps a player choose an action. A priority order makes a received hit or low hull easier to notice among effects, ships and objectives.
decisions.tradeoff: A quieter interface can hide context that an experienced player wants. The map and overview must provide a dependable route to that detail, and the priority policy needs human playtesting.

outcome: I separated immediate battle awareness, fleet spending and tactical inspection across the combat view, Fleet drawer and overview. The prototype supports solo AI-filled matches and crew rooms in one capture-and-hold arena. The captures here show the actual game; the illustrated harbor is menu artwork.
reflection: I would put a new crew through requesting a repair, spending supplies and choosing a relay without coaching. Missed requests and time spent searching the overview would help me decide what to simplify next.
nextSteps: Proposed playtest: form two crews and ask players to explain their role, request or buy a repair, and identify the relay that matters next without coaching.
Proposed checks: invitation and room entry, role reassignment, a guest disconnecting, restrictive peer-to-peer networks, and an honest explanation when a host leaves.
Proposed observations: missed requests, map-to-world confusion, unnoticed critical alerts and time spent in the overview. Compare these before changing the attention policy.

name: Halo
headline: Keep the action close to the pointer.
summary: A desktop action ring for frequently used shortcuts, with app-specific layouts and a visual editor.
role: Interaction direction, action organisation & configuration UX
problem: A useful shortcut is one I can reach without breaking the task I am doing. Halo puts a ring of actions around the pointer, instead of asking me to hunt through menus or remember another keyboard combination. The design problem was keeping that first choice quick while still allowing the ring to grow.
process: I organised the experience around opening the ring, choosing a direction and returning to the original task. Clicking supports a deliberate choice; holding the shortcut, moving towards an action and releasing supports a quicker gesture once the layout is familiar.

The editor exposes the same ring spatially. Selecting a slot opens its action, app behaviour, label and appearance settings. App-specific rings and folders hold more choices without putting every action into the first ring.

Halo is an independent project inspired by Logitech’s Actions Ring. I focused on the interaction and visual configuration. Comparing click and flick selection with familiar keyboard shortcuts is still a useful next test.

decisions.title: Make the first choice spatial
decisions.choice: Keep actions in stable positions around the pointer, with labels available while choosing.
decisions.reason: A direction can become familiar through use, while labels help someone who is still learning the layout.
decisions.tradeoff: Moving actions frequently would work against that familiarity. Customisation needs to feel deliberate.

decisions.title: Let the editor mirror the ring
decisions.choice: Select a slot in the ring and edit that action beside it.
decisions.reason: The person can see which position they are changing instead of translating between a list and the final layout.
decisions.tradeoff: A visual editor still needs clear names and keyboard access; position alone is not enough.

decisions.title: Keep specialised actions out of the first layer
decisions.choice: Use app-specific rings and folders for actions that belong to a particular context.
decisions.reason: A general ring can stay small while a specialist workflow has its own useful choices.
decisions.tradeoff: Context changes and nested folders must remain predictable. More actions do not automatically make the tool faster.

outcome: I gave the ring and its editor the same spatial model, with click and hold-and-flick selection, per-app configurations and nested action folders. The app supports actions such as app control, media, window management and snippets. Some actions depend on the operating system and the permissions available.
reflection: I would start a comparison with a small, familiar task set rather than a ring full of possibilities. I want to know which positions people remember, when they hesitate and whether app-specific rings help or surprise them.
nextSteps: Proposed study: configure three frequently used actions, repeat the task after a break and compare hesitation with an existing shortcut method.
Proposed checks: keyboard-only configuration, ring changes between apps, folder backtracking and permission-denied actions.

name: Binnder
headline: Review the file. Keep a way back.
summary: A native Android file-review app that combines large previews with explicit keep, bin and permanent-delete actions.
role: File-review flow, destructive-action UX & information hierarchy
problem: Storage cleanup is easy to rush and difficult to undo. I wanted the file itself to be the main thing on screen, with a clear difference between keeping it, moving it to a bin and deleting it permanently. The interaction should make those consequences visible before a gesture becomes an operation.
process: I put the largest files first and used a large preview with fixed actions. File-type filters help narrow the queue, while matching buttons and accessibility actions make swiping optional.

I separated reversible binning from permanent deletion. An upward swipe asks for confirmation, and every deletion action has a five-second Undo window before the operation begins. A kept file is hidden from review for seven days rather than treated as permanently resolved.

The bin reports its retention period and supports preview and restore. Moving a file there does not free storage, so the interface must not count those bytes as recovered space. The captures use sample portfolio files in a separate emulator, not a scan of someone’s phone.

decisions.title: Keep the file visible while deciding
decisions.choice: Use a large preview, file name, size and fixed Keep, Bin and Delete forever controls.
decisions.reason: The decision should be about a recognisable file, not an unfamiliar path in a long list.
decisions.tradeoff: Some formats need another installed app. The preview must explain that limitation without implying a file is broken.

decisions.title: Give permanent deletion its own commitment
decisions.choice: Ask for confirmation and name the file before queuing permanent deletion, then offer the individual Undo window.
decisions.reason: A gesture alone is too easy to misinterpret when the result cannot be recovered through the app.
decisions.tradeoff: Extra confirmation slows cleanup. It belongs to the more consequential action rather than every decision.

decisions.title: Describe the bin honestly
decisions.choice: Show retention and restoration separately from bytes actually deleted.
decisions.reason: A recoverable file still occupies storage. The person needs to understand both recovery and capacity.
decisions.tradeoff: Retention depends on the device being able to run cleanup and reach the volume; it is not an exact deletion appointment.

outcome: I designed one-file-at-a-time review with visible alternatives to gestures, a recoverable bin and an explicit permanent-delete path. The native app also accounts for interrupted operations and changed files. I still need to check those recovery paths across Android devices and removable storage.
reflection: I would test a mistaken swipe, a removed storage volume and a restore destination that already exists. A cleanup tool earns trust when it explains what happened and preserves a way to recover, especially when it cannot finish an operation.
nextSteps: Proposed study: review a small set of test files, undo an unintended action and restore a file without coaching.
Proposed checks: permission loss, app restart during a pending action, missing SD card and a file changed since scanning.

name: PureEQ
headline: Find a sound you can adjust and keep.
summary: An Android sound-tuning app that combines a per-ear listening check, music preferences and editable EQ profiles.
role: Setup journey, listening-test interaction & profile controls
problem: A row of equaliser sliders assumes that someone already knows which frequencies they want to change. I approached PureEQ as a guided starting point: explain the setup, gather a few listening responses, compare music and leave the result open to adjustment.
process: I separated the listening check from the taste test. The first asks whether a short tone is audible through the current headphones; the second asks which of two music treatments the person prefers. Neither needs to be presented as an expert diagnosis.

Preparation is part of the flow: a quiet environment, suitable headphones, stable volume and a left/right check. The result can then be adjusted with named controls, compared with EQ off and saved as a profile.

Export gives the profile a useful life beyond the setup. The documented formats have different capabilities, so a combined curve or per-ear adjustment needs explanation. The captures show the actual native starting flow, not a completed hearing test or a clinical result.

decisions.title: Explain the two kinds of input
decisions.choice: Describe listening responses and music preferences as separate steps before asking for either.
decisions.reason: A person should know whether they are reporting audibility or choosing a sound they like.
decisions.tradeoff: A short explanation must not make the listening check sound like a calibrated audiogram.

decisions.title: Leave the suggestion editable
decisions.choice: Offer named fine-tuning controls, an EQ on/off comparison and a way back to suggested settings.
decisions.reason: The suggested curve is a starting point. People need to hear and revise it rather than accept it as an unquestionable result.
decisions.tradeoff: Several controls can become confusing together. Reset and suggested-value feedback need to make changes traceable.

decisions.title: Carry context into export
decisions.choice: Describe the target format and explain when an app combines left and right curves.
decisions.reason: A technically valid export can still behave differently from the per-ear result shown in PureEQ.
decisions.tradeoff: Compatibility depends on the receiving app and device. Exporting a file does not guarantee the same playback everywhere.

outcome: I connected preparation, listening responses, A/B choices and an editable result into a profile flow. The app can apply the EQ or export it for another player, with limitations explained for each format. This is personal sound tuning, not a clinical hearing assessment.
reflection: I would test whether people can tell what came from their listening responses, what came from preference choices and what they changed afterwards. If those differences are unclear, the final curve may look more certain than it should.
nextSteps: Proposed study: complete setup with headphones, explain each stage and compare a saved result with EQ off at matched loudness.
Proposed checks: interrupted setup, a volume change, incorrect channel identification, resetting one adjustment and exporting a combined curve.

name: Hidden Identity Chess
headline: Familiar chess. Very different information.
summary: A digital adaptation of Hidden Identity Chess, with private setup, bluffing, challenges and a focused play surface.
role: Digital adaptation, private setup & game interaction design
context: Independent adaptation · Triple S Games rules
problem: A familiar chessboard is useful orientation, but it can also create the wrong expectations when piece identities are hidden and bluffing is allowed. I focused the adaptation on explaining what is private, what a player can do now and how a challenge changes the game.
process: I separated arranging an army from playing it. In same-device mode, a covered handoff protects the next player’s view. Online play needs the same distinction in what each player receives, not just a visual cover over shared data.

Zen mode keeps the board, players, turn and Move, Bluff and Challenge controls in view. History, hints and secondary tools move into sheets so they can be inspected without permanently shrinking the board.

The rules and original game concept are credited to Triple S Games. This is an independent digital adaptation. I treated computer play, shared-device play and online rooms as separate flows because they have different privacy and connection requirements.

decisions.title: Make hidden information explicit
decisions.choice: Show the player’s own identities and keep the opponent’s pieces visually hidden.
decisions.reason: Someone should understand the information available to each side before making a move.
decisions.tradeoff: Shared-device privacy depends on a clear handoff; it cannot stop someone looking at the screen at the wrong time.

decisions.title: Name the unusual actions
decisions.choice: Keep Move, Bluff and Challenge as separate controls with rules available nearby.
decisions.reason: The familiar board should not make a new player assume ordinary check-and-checkmate behaviour.
decisions.tradeoff: A challenge can refer to earlier play, so its target and consequence need careful explanation.

decisions.title: Give the board the space
decisions.choice: Use the focused play view and move history and secondary tools into deliberate inspection surfaces.
decisions.reason: The board is easier to read when optional tools do not compete for its space.
decisions.tradeoff: Hiding history can make challenges harder to investigate. The route back to a past move must remain obvious.

outcome: I designed setup, private handoff and the focused game view around the information each player can use. The game supports computer, same-device and online play, with explicit challenge controls and local saving. I still want to test whether a new player understands the handoff and can investigate a challenge.
reflection: I would watch where an experienced chess player applies an ordinary rule that does not belong here. Those moments would tell me where the adaptation needs a clearer explanation rather than another hint.
nextSteps: Proposed study: arrange an army, make a bluff and investigate a past move with a first-time player.
Proposed checks: shared-device handoff, keyboard square navigation, a disconnected online player and restoring a local game.

name: 5 Dead
headline: Keep the table moving. Keep the turn clear.
summary: An independent digital card game with bot play, shared-device turns and online rooms, built around a visible running total and card actions.
role: Game presentation, joining flow & turn feedback
problem: A card table has several things to explain at once: the current total, whose turn it is, what a card will do and who is still in the hand. I wanted the presentation to give each moment a clear focus without making players work through a rules panel on every turn.
process: I kept the running total and current discard near the centre, opponents around the table and the local hand close to the player. Selection and a Play action help separate considering a card from committing it.

The three entry modes make different promises. Bot play and local pass-and-play can work offline after the app is ready; online rooms depend on a connection and wait for a disconnected player. Shared-device turns use a privacy screen between hands.

This is an independent game inspired by Hasbro’s 5 Alive. Larger tables use a disclosed house rule. The generated arena and card artwork are assets used in the game itself; I kept the running total, hand and turn feedback distinct from that background.

decisions.title: Keep the running total central
decisions.choice: Place the total, discard and turn state where the next decision is made.
decisions.reason: A player needs to connect the chosen card to the current state of the hand.
decisions.tradeoff: Effects and animations can obscure that relationship if they linger or hide the next turn.

decisions.title: Separate choosing from playing
decisions.choice: Show a selected card and an explicit Play action, alongside the supported drag interaction.
decisions.reason: Considering a card should not accidentally commit it, especially on a crowded phone hand.
decisions.tradeoff: An extra action can slow experienced play. Both methods need clear feedback and usable touch targets.

decisions.title: Explain the mode before the table starts
decisions.choice: Distinguish bot, pass-and-play and connected rooms, including their waiting and privacy states.
decisions.reason: A group should know whether it needs one device, several devices or a network before starting.
decisions.tradeoff: Local privacy covers are a social convention; online connection loss can pause the table.

outcome: I brought the hand, table, turn feedback and joining flow into one playable presentation. Bot and local play work separately from connected rooms. Larger tables follow the documented house rules, with waiting and privacy states suited to each mode.
reflection: I would test the smallest phone hand and the largest table before adding more effects. The useful questions are whether the next player notices their turn and whether someone can tell what a special card just changed.
nextSteps: Proposed study: start a bot hand, play a special card and explain the next action without opening the full rules.
Proposed checks: overlapping cards, shared-device handoff, a disconnected seat and the clarity of the extended-table rule.

name: Alibi
headline: Watch privately. Give just enough away.
summary: A social video-imposter game that takes a group through private clips, one-word clues, discussion, voting and a reveal.
role: Game direction, private-viewing flow & group interaction design
problem: A social-deduction game loses its rhythm when someone misses a step or sees information too soon. Alibi gives most players the same clip and one player a related alternative, then moves the group through clues, discussion and voting. The flow needs to protect the mystery without making the group wait without an explanation.
process: I structured each round as private viewing, one-word submission, shared clues, discussion, a hidden vote and the reveal. Players need a shared phase and a private view at the same time.

I used a solo practice path with clearly labelled simulated opponents so the whole sequence can be tried before inviting friends. A practice lobby should not look like proof that other people are connected.

The project includes room chat and built-in calling, with external calls as another option. Playback depends on YouTube availability and embedding, and the server keeps room state in memory. Those limits make readiness, replacement clips and host recovery controls part of the design.

decisions.title: Keep private viewing separate from the group phase
decisions.choice: Show each assigned clip privately and release clues together after submission or timeout.
decisions.reason: Early clues or role information could change the game before everyone has had a chance to act.
decisions.tradeoff: A shared phase still needs a clear explanation when a player is loading or has not submitted.

decisions.title: Make practice an honest invitation
decisions.choice: Label simulated players throughout solo practice and let the person try the real sequence.
decisions.reason: Someone can learn the rhythm without assembling a group or mistaking demo activity for real participants.
decisions.tradeoff: Practice can explain controls but cannot reproduce the conversation and hesitation of a group.

decisions.title: Explain waits and recovery
decisions.choice: Keep the current phase, readiness and host controls visible when playback or connection needs attention.
decisions.reason: The group needs a next action rather than an unexplained delay.
decisions.tradeoff: A replacement clip or returning player can affect the round. The interface needs to say when play restarts instead of hiding that change.

outcome: I connected the lobby, private watching, clues, discussion, votes and reveal into one group flow. Solo practice explains the steps with simulated opponents; connected rooms support real players. A study with a real group is the next step for evaluating the social experience.
reflection: I would watch a real group through a failed clip and a late player, not just a successful reveal. Those pauses would show whether the instructions preserve the social rhythm or turn the host into technical support.
nextSteps: Proposed study: run a short group session and observe phase explanations, accidental information sharing and waiting time.
Proposed checks: a blocked YouTube embed, a reconnecting player, a departing host and switching between built-in and external calling.
